DIS.what: Sells entertainment - films, streaming, linear TV, theme parks and cruises - and licenses its characters.
DIS.rev: Experiences (parks and cruises) ~37% of revenue but the majority of operating profit; entertainment (studios, Disney+, linear) ~45%; sports (ESPN) ~18%.
DIS.gm: Parks carry high incremental margins on fixed assets; streaming has only recently turned profitable; linear TV is in structural decline.
DIS.mgmt: Josh D'Amaro is CEO after the long-running Iger succession question was resolved. Insider ownership minimal.
DIS.comp: Netflix and YouTube for streaming attention, Universal and Comcast in parks, sports rights bidders for ESPN.
DIS.moat: Irreplaceable intellectual property - a century of characters - plus theme park real estate that cannot be rebuilt.
DIS.ind: Parks demand is solid; linear TV is shrinking fast; streaming is growing but crowded.
DIS.risk: Cord-cutting accelerating faster than ESPN direct-to-consumer can replace, plus a consumer slowdown hitting parks.
DIS.implied: A high-teens to low-20s P/E implies streaming margins keep improving and parks growth holds.
DIS.debate: Bulls say the IP plus parks combination is unrepeatable and streaming profits are just starting. Bears see a melting linear ice cube and succession risk.
DIS.disprove: Linear networks revenue falling faster than guided; parks per-capita spending declining; streaming margin expansion stalling; ESPN direct launch disappointing.

PEP.what: Sells snacks (Frito-Lay, Quaker) and beverages (Pepsi, Gatorade) to consumers through retailers, globally.
PEP.rev: Convenient foods roughly 55% of profit, beverages the rest. North America is about 60% of revenue. Frito-Lay is the crown jewel.
PEP.gm: Gross margin around 54-55%. Snacks carry better economics than beverages because of direct store delivery and shelf control.
PEP.mgmt: Ramon Laguarta is CEO. Insider ownership minimal; an activist has pushed for portfolio changes.
PEP.comp: Coca-Cola and Keurig Dr Pepper in drinks; Mondelez, Kellanova, General Mills and private label in snacks.
PEP.moat: Direct store delivery network, brand portfolio and shelf space that a new entrant cannot buy.
PEP.ind: Snacking volumes in North America have been weak - the first real volume decline in years.
PEP.risk: GLP-1 medication adoption structurally reducing snack consumption, which would attack the most profitable half of the company.
PEP.implied: A high-teens P/E implies a return to mid single-digit organic growth after volume declines - the market is not fully convinced.
PEP.debate: Bulls say the valuation already reflects the volume problem and Frito-Lay pricing power is intact. Bears say the salty snack category has a structural demand question.
PEP.disprove: Frito-Lay North America volumes negative for several more quarters; price/mix contribution shrinking; market share loss to private label.

SCHW.what: Runs a retail brokerage and custody platform, and earns most of its profit as a bank on client cash balances.
SCHW.rev: Net interest revenue on client cash roughly half, asset management fees ~30%, trading ~15%. US retail and adviser clients.
SCHW.gm: Watch net interest margin, cash sorting behaviour and pre-tax profit margin (40%+ in good conditions).
SCHW.mgmt: Rick Wurster became CEO in 2025. Insider ownership modest; the Ameritrade integration is complete.
SCHW.comp: Fidelity, Vanguard, Interactive Brokers, Robinhood and the wirehouses in advisory custody.
SCHW.moat: Scale in custody and a client base whose cash sits at the bank by default - the sweep is the profit engine, and inertia protects it.
SCHW.ind: Retail investing participation keeps growing; cash sorting is the cyclical variable.
SCHW.risk: A rate environment where clients keep moving cash to money market funds, squeezing the spread that most of the profit comes from.
SCHW.implied: A low-20s P/E implies cash sorting has ended and net interest margin expands from here.
SCHW.debate: Bulls say deposit costs normalising plus asset growth means years of earnings expansion. Bears note the 2023 episode showed how rate-sensitive the model is.
SCHW.disprove: Bank sweep balances declining; net interest margin not expanding; new account growth slowing; clients shifting to higher-yield alternatives.

DE.what: Sells agricultural, construction and forestry machinery, plus precision agriculture technology, with captive financing.
DE.rev: Production and precision agriculture ~35%, small agriculture and turf ~22%, construction and forestry ~25%, financial services the rest. US and Canada ~55%.
DE.gm: Gross margin around 28-32%. Dealer network and parts drive profitability, and precision ag software is being layered on as a subscription.
DE.mgmt: John May is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company manages production tightly to dealer inventory.
DE.comp: CNH Industrial, AGCO, Kubota in agriculture; Caterpillar and Komatsu in construction.
DE.moat: Dealer network, brand loyalty among farmers, and a precision ag data platform that raises switching costs beyond the iron.
DE.ind: Agriculture is in a downcycle: low crop prices mean farmers defer equipment purchases.
DE.risk: A prolonged farm income recession keeping large equipment sales at trough levels for several years.
DE.implied: A P/E in the 20s on trough earnings implies a cyclical recovery in farm incomes within a couple of years.
DE.debate: Bulls say Deere manages the downcycle better than ever and precision ag adds recurring revenue. Bears say ag cycles last longer than investors expect.
DE.disprove: Large ag equipment orders falling further; used equipment prices declining; farm income forecasts cut; precision ag subscriptions not scaling.

MCD.what: Franchises and operates quick-service restaurants - it is largely a real estate and royalty business with a burger brand attached.
MCD.rev: About 95% of restaurants are franchised; revenue is rent and royalties plus company-operated sales. International operated and developmental markets are over half of operating income.
MCD.gm: Franchised margins run above 80% because the revenue is rent and a percentage of sales with minimal cost. Company-operated margins are far lower.
MCD.mgmt: Chris Kempczinski is CEO. Insider ownership minimal; the dividend has risen every year since 1976.
MCD.comp: Burger King (RBI), Wendys, Chick-fil-A, Yum Brands, plus local chains internationally.
MCD.moat: Brand recognition at global scale, prime real estate locations, franchisee economics that attract the best operators, and purchasing scale.
MCD.ind: Low-income consumer traffic has been weak; value menus are defending share at the cost of mix.
MCD.risk: A sustained traffic decline among lower-income consumers that value pricing cannot fix without damaging franchisee profitability.
MCD.implied: A mid-20s P/E implies low single-digit comparable sales growth plus unit expansion and buybacks - modest but requires traffic to stabilise.
MCD.debate: Bulls say it is the most defensive consumer brand with an inflation-linked rent stream. Bears point at negative US traffic and GLP-1 headwinds.
MCD.disprove: US comparable sales negative on traffic rather than price; franchisee margin complaints; international developmental markets slowing; unit growth guidance cut.

T.what: Sells mobile and fibre broadband connectivity to US consumers and businesses.
T.rev: Mobility ~70%, business wireline ~15% (declining), consumer wireline and fibre ~15% (growing). US only.
T.gm: Capital intensity is the story: EBITDA margins in the 30s-40s but fibre build and spectrum consume the cash.
T.mgmt: John Stankey is CEO and has refocused on connectivity after the failed media acquisitions. Insider ownership minimal.
T.comp: Verizon, T-Mobile, cable operators in broadband and mobile.
T.moat: Spectrum, fibre footprint and scale. Fibre is the genuinely advantaged asset because it is expensive to overbuild.
T.ind: Mature wireless; fibre passings are a multi-year growth project.
T.risk: A wireless price war, or the fibre build costing more per home passed than the returns justify.
T.implied: A low-to-mid teens P/E implies steady subscriber growth and free cash flow funding the dividend and debt paydown.
T.debate: Bulls say deleveraging plus fibre growth with a covered dividend. Bears remember a decade of value destruction and heavy debt.
T.disprove: Fibre net adds slowing; postpaid phone churn rising; free cash flow guidance missed; net debt to EBITDA not improving.

GILD.what: Sells HIV treatment and prevention medicines, plus oncology and liver disease drugs.
GILD.rev: HIV is roughly 70% of product sales, led by Biktarvy, with lenacapavir (Yeztugo) the major new prevention launch. Oncology and liver the rest. US ~70%.
GILD.gm: Gross margin around 76-79%. Patented antivirals with strong US pricing, partially offset by government programme rebates.
GILD.mgmt: Daniel ODay is CEO. Insider ownership small; acquisitions in oncology have had mixed results.
GILD.comp: ViiV (GSK) in HIV, Merck in HIV prevention, plus a wide field in oncology.
GILD.moat: HIV franchise dominance with proven regimens physicians will not switch casually, patents to the 2030s, and manufacturing scale.
GILD.ind: HIV treatment is stable and growing slowly; long-acting prevention is a genuinely new market.
GILD.risk: Biktarvy losing exclusivity in the early 2030s without lenacapavir scaling to replace it, or US prevention funding being cut.
GILD.implied: A mid-teens P/E implies modest growth with the lenacapavir launch partly credited - not a heroic assumption.
GILD.debate: Bulls say twice-yearly HIV prevention is a category-defining product with a durable cash franchise behind it. Bears point to a patent cliff and a weak oncology record.
GILD.disprove: Yeztugo uptake slower than launch trajectory; Biktarvy growth stalling; oncology write-downs; Medicaid and PEPFAR funding reductions.

ABT.what: Sells medical devices (continuous glucose monitors, cardiac devices), diagnostics, nutrition products and generic medicines.
ABT.rev: Medical devices ~45% and the growth engine, established pharmaceuticals ~17%, nutrition ~17%, diagnostics ~20%. Roughly 40% US.
ABT.gm: Gross margin around 55-57%. Devices like FreeStyle Libre carry strong margins and recurring consumable revenue.
ABT.mgmt: Robert Ford is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company has an unusually balanced portfolio by design.
ABT.comp: Dexcom in glucose monitoring, Medtronic and Boston Scientific in cardiac, Roche and Siemens in diagnostics, Danone in nutrition.
ABT.moat: FreeStyle Libre scale and prescriber habit, regulatory approvals, and hospital relationships across four different businesses.
ABT.ind: Diabetes technology is growing strongly; diagnostics has normalised after COVID; nutrition is mature.
ABT.risk: Reimbursement pressure or a competitive CGM price war with Dexcom and new entrants compressing the best segment.
ABT.implied: A mid-20s P/E implies high single-digit organic growth led by devices.
ABT.debate: Bulls like the diversification and the Libre growth runway into basal and non-insulin users. Bears see litigation over preterm infant formula and slower diagnostics.
ABT.disprove: Libre growth decelerating below 15%; CGM pricing falling; nutrition litigation verdicts; diagnostics revenue declining.

ADI.what: Sells high-performance analog and mixed-signal chips to industrial, automotive, communications and healthcare customers.
ADI.rev: Industrial ~45%, automotive ~30%, communications ~11%, consumer ~12%. Broadly global with a large European and Asian base.
ADI.gm: Gross margin around 57-60%. Long product lifecycles, proprietary designs and a hybrid manufacturing model support the margin.
ADI.mgmt: Vincent Roche has been CEO since 2013. Insider ownership small; the Maxim acquisition was well executed.
ADI.comp: Texas Instruments, Infineon, NXP, STMicroelectronics, Microchip.
ADI.moat: Analog parts designed into industrial systems for a decade or more - once specified, they are rarely re-qualified - plus deep applications engineering.
ADI.ind: Industrial semiconductors are recovering from a deep inventory correction; auto content keeps rising.
ADI.risk: Industrial capex staying weak while automotive production declines - both core markets soft at once.
ADI.implied: A high-30s P/E implies a full cyclical recovery plus continued content growth.
ADI.debate: Bulls say ADI is the highest-quality analog franchise with the best industrial exposure. Bears say the multiple already assumes the recovery is complete.
ADI.disprove: Bookings not improving; industrial revenue still declining; automotive orders cut; inventory at distributors rising.

BLK.what: Manages money - index funds, ETFs, active strategies and now private markets and infrastructure - for institutions and individuals.
BLK.rev: Investment advisory and administration fees from over $12 trillion of assets, plus technology services (Aladdin) which is a high-multiple software business inside an asset manager.
BLK.gm: Operating margin around 38-45%. Asset management is a scale business: the incremental dollar of assets costs almost nothing to manage.
BLK.mgmt: Larry Fink is co-founder and CEO; succession is the key governance question. Insider ownership modest.
BLK.comp: Vanguard and State Street in index, Blackstone and KKR in private markets, Fidelity across the board.
BLK.moat: Scale that makes iShares fee competition survivable, Aladdin embedded in client risk systems, and distribution relationships everywhere.
BLK.ind: Passive flows keep growing; private markets and infrastructure are the higher-fee growth frontier.
BLK.risk: A severe market drawdown cutting the asset base and therefore fees, or fee compression accelerating faster than flows.
BLK.implied: A mid-20s P/E implies continued net inflows plus a successful shift into higher-fee private assets.
BLK.debate: Bulls say Aladdin plus private markets justify a premium to asset-manager multiples. Bears note fee rates keep falling and the business is levered to market levels.
BLK.disprove: Net outflows in a rising market; effective fee rate falling faster than asset growth; private markets acquisitions not delivering targeted fee income.

NEE.what: Runs Florida Power and Light, a large regulated utility, and NextEra Energy Resources, the largest renewables developer in the US.
NEE.rev: FPL regulated utility roughly two-thirds of earnings, Energy Resources (wind, solar, storage, nuclear) the rest and the growth engine.
NEE.gm: Regulated utilities earn an allowed return on rate base - roughly 10-11% - so growth comes from investing capital, not from margin.
NEE.mgmt: John Ketchum is CEO. Insider ownership small; the business is capital-intensive and financed with heavy debt issuance.
NEE.comp: Other utilities and independent power producers; in renewables, everyone from oil majors to infrastructure funds.
NEE.moat: Regulated monopoly in Florida, a development pipeline and interconnection queue position that took decades to assemble, and financing scale.
NEE.ind: Electricity demand is growing again after twenty flat years - data centres and electrification.
NEE.risk: Federal clean energy tax credit rollbacks plus higher interest rates making the renewables development model less profitable.
NEE.implied: A low-20s P/E for a utility implies above-average earnings growth (6-8%) continuing.
NEE.debate: Bulls say it owns the best regulated jurisdiction and the largest renewables pipeline in a demand upcycle. Bears point at rate sensitivity, debt and policy risk.
NEE.disprove: Renewables backlog additions slowing; tax credit legislation changes; FPL rate case outcome below expectations; credit rating pressure.

UNP.what: Runs the western US freight rail network, hauling intermodal containers, grain, coal, chemicals and cars.
UNP.rev: Bulk (grain, coal, fertiliser) ~33%, industrial ~35%, premium (intermodal and automotive) ~32%. Western two-thirds of the US plus Mexico gateways.
UNP.gm: Operating ratio is the metric - around 58-60%, meaning 40%+ operating margin. Rail is a fixed-cost business where volume is everything.
UNP.mgmt: Jim Vena is CEO. Insider ownership small; the pending combination with Norfolk Southern would create the first transcontinental railroad.
UNP.comp: BNSF (Berkshire) in the west, trucking for shorter hauls, and the eastern railroads at interchange points.
UNP.moat: Rights of way that cannot be rebuilt at any price, and a duopoly structure in the western US. This is one of the most durable moats in the market.
UNP.ind: Volumes track industrial production and are structurally flat to slightly up; pricing above inflation is the earnings driver.
UNP.risk: The Norfolk Southern merger being blocked or conditioned heavily by the Surface Transportation Board, or a freight recession.
UNP.implied: A low-20s P/E implies pricing power holds and merger synergies are eventually realised.
UNP.debate: Bulls say irreplaceable assets, pricing above inflation and a transformative merger. Bears note volume growth has been near zero for a decade.
UNP.disprove: Carload volumes declining; operating ratio deteriorating; merger denied or heavily conditioned; truck capacity undercutting rail pricing.

WELL.what: Owns senior housing, outpatient medical and health system real estate, and takes operating upside in its senior housing portfolio.
WELL.rev: Senior housing operating portfolio is the majority and the growth engine; triple-net leases and outpatient medical the rest. US, Canada and the UK.
WELL.gm: REIT metrics: watch funds from operations per share, same-store net operating income growth (running high single to low double digits) and occupancy.
WELL.mgmt: Shankh Mitra is CEO. Insider ownership modest; the company has been an aggressive and so far successful acquirer.
WELL.comp: Ventas, Healthpeak, Brookdale as an operator, and private capital bidding for the same assets.
WELL.moat: Scale in senior housing data and operator relationships, plus a cost of capital advantage that lets it buy assets others cannot.
WELL.ind: The 80-plus population is growing rapidly while new senior housing construction is at a multi-decade low - the best supply-demand setup in real estate.
WELL.risk: A wave of new construction starting, or labour cost inflation in senior housing outrunning rent growth.
WELL.implied: A high multiple of funds from operations implies occupancy keeps climbing toward pre-pandemic levels with strong rent growth.
WELL.debate: Bulls say demographics plus no new supply equals years of double-digit net operating income growth. Bears say the valuation already reflects it and REITs are rate-sensitive.
WELL.disprove: Same-store occupancy gains stalling; senior housing construction starts rising; labour costs accelerating; acquisitions at cap rates below cost of capital.

BA.what: Builds commercial aircraft, defence systems and space hardware for airlines and governments.
BA.rev: Commercial airplanes ~40%, defence and space ~35%, global services ~25% and the only consistently profitable segment.
BA.gm: Commercial aircraft margins have been negative for years due to production problems and charges; services carries the profit.
BA.mgmt: Kelly Ortberg became CEO in 2024 to fix quality and production. Insider ownership small; the balance sheet carries heavy debt.
BA.comp: Airbus in commercial (now the clear leader), Lockheed and Northrop in defence.
BA.moat: A duopoly in large commercial aircraft with certification barriers that are effectively absolute, plus an installed base needing parts for decades.
BA.ind: Airlines want far more aircraft than the duopoly can build - demand is not the problem, production is.
BA.risk: Another quality or safety incident resetting production rates and FAA oversight again.
BA.implied: The price implies production rates recover to 737 MAX rates above 50 a month and free cash flow returns to prior levels.
BA.debate: Bulls say a duopoly with a decade-long backlog cannot stay broken forever. Bears note years of promises, dilution and negative cash flow.
BA.disprove: Monthly delivery rates not climbing; new charges on fixed-price defence contracts; FAA rate caps extended; free cash flow still negative.

COP.what: Produces oil and gas from a large, low-cost portfolio spanning the Permian, Alaska, Norway and LNG projects.
COP.rev: Lower 48 (Permian, Eagle Ford, Bakken) is the bulk; Alaska, Canada, Norway, Qatar LNG and Asia Pacific the rest.
COP.gm: Watch cash cost per barrel and the free cash flow break-even, which ConocoPhillips targets around $40 WTI.
COP.mgmt: Andrew O'Brien is CEO, succeeding Ryan Lance. Insider ownership small; the company is explicit about returning a large share of cash flow to shareholders.
COP.comp: ExxonMobil, Chevron, EOG, Occidental and other large independents.
COP.moat: Low cost of supply across a deep inventory - the moat in commodities is being the low-cost producer, not having pricing power.
COP.ind: Oil demand growth is modest; US shale productivity gains are slowing; LNG demand is growing.
COP.risk: Oil below $55 combined with the large capital commitments to Willow and LNG projects.
COP.implied: The multiple implies mid-cycle oil and the major projects delivering on budget.
COP.debate: Bulls like the low break-even and disciplined distributions. Bears note the capex on Willow and LNG comes before the cash flow.
COP.disprove: Break-even rising; Willow cost overruns; distributions cut when oil falls; production guidance missed.

PFE.what: Sells prescription medicines and vaccines - COVID products, oncology after the Seagen acquisition, and a broad primary care portfolio.
PFE.rev: Primary care (including Comirnaty and Paxlovid), specialty care and oncology. COVID revenue is volatile and declining. US around half.
PFE.gm: Gross margin around 65-70%, dragged by COVID product write-offs and the cost of acquired oncology assets.
PFE.mgmt: Albert Bourla is CEO. Insider ownership small; the Seagen deal added significant debt and is the defining capital allocation decision.
PFE.comp: Merck, AstraZeneca, BMS in oncology; Moderna in vaccines; GSK in respiratory.
PFE.moat: Scale in manufacturing and regulatory affairs, patents on the oncology portfolio, and vaccine distribution reach.
PFE.ind: Post-COVID normalisation is over; the issue now is a 2026-2028 patent cliff across several large products.
PFE.risk: The Seagen oncology pipeline failing to offset the loss of exclusivity on Eliquis, Ibrance and Xeljanz.
PFE.implied: A single-digit to low-teens P/E and a high dividend yield imply the market expects the cliff to win.
PFE.debate: Bulls say a cheap multiple with a covered dividend and an underrated oncology pipeline. Bears say the pipeline has to replace roughly $15bn of revenue and has not proven it can.
PFE.disprove: Oncology readouts failing; net debt not declining; dividend coverage from free cash flow deteriorating; cost cuts not reaching guidance.

IBKR.what: Runs an electronic brokerage for active traders, professional investors and introducing brokers worldwide.
IBKR.rev: Net interest income on client cash and margin loans is roughly two-thirds; commissions the rest. Truly global client base across 200+ countries.
IBKR.gm: Pre-tax margin above 70% - among the highest of any listed financial - because the platform is automated and headcount grows slowly.
IBKR.mgmt: Founder Thomas Peterffy still controls the majority of the company; Milan Galik is CEO. Founder alignment is total.
IBKR.comp: Charles Schwab, Robinhood, Futu and Tiger in Asia, plus local brokers such as UOB Kay Hian and Moomoo in Singapore.
IBKR.moat: Lowest-cost automated infrastructure, global market access in one account, and a cost base that barely moves as accounts grow.
IBKR.ind: Global retail and professional trading participation keeps growing, especially outside the US.
IBKR.risk: A sharp fall in interest rates cutting the interest income that is most of the profit, combined with quieter markets.
IBKR.implied: A high-20s to 30s P/E implies continued 20%+ account growth and no severe rate-driven earnings decline.
IBKR.debate: Bulls say it is the lowest-cost global broker compounding accounts at 30% a year. Bears note profits are levered to rates and market activity.
IBKR.disprove: Account growth slowing below 20%; client credit balances falling; net interest margin compressing sharply; commission per trade declining.

WDC.what: Sells hard disk drives - now almost entirely for data centre mass storage after spinning off the flash business.
WDC.rev: Nearline HDD for cloud and enterprise is the dominant revenue source; client and consumer drives the remainder.
WDC.gm: Gross margin has risen sharply in the current upcycle as HDD supply is tight and pricing has improved - it is a two-player market with Seagate.
WDC.mgmt: Irving Tan leads the post-separation company. Insider ownership small; capital discipline is the promise of the new structure.
WDC.comp: Seagate is effectively the only competitor; flash-based SSDs compete at the margin for some workloads.
WDC.moat: A duopoly in high-capacity drives with enormous technology barriers (HAMR and SMR) and disciplined capacity - the best structure HDD has ever had.
WDC.ind: AI data storage demand has lifted nearline drive demand after years of decline.
WDC.risk: Flash prices falling far enough to displace HDD in mass storage tiers, or cloud customers digesting inventory after a buying surge.
WDC.implied: The price implies the current tight supply and pricing persist rather than mean-revert.
WDC.debate: Bulls say AI creates permanent demand for cheap bulk storage and the duopoly is disciplined. Bears say storage has always been cyclical and margins are at records.
WDC.disprove: Exabyte shipment growth slowing; pricing per terabyte falling; cloud customers extending drive replacement cycles; capacity additions announced.

BX.what: Manages private equity, real estate, credit and infrastructure funds for institutions and, increasingly, wealthy individuals.
BX.rev: Management fees (stable) plus performance revenues (volatile) across over $1 trillion of assets under management. Real estate and credit are the largest pools.
BX.gm: Fee-related earnings margin above 55%. The economics are excellent when fundraising works and realisations happen.
BX.mgmt: Co-founder Stephen Schwarzman is chairman and CEO with a large stake; Jon Gray is president and the likely successor.
BX.comp: KKR, Apollo, Brookfield, Ares and the largest sovereign and pension funds investing directly.
BX.moat: Brand and track record that make fundraising easier, scale that allows deals nobody else can do, and long lock-up capital.
BX.ind: Private markets keep taking share of institutional portfolios; the wealth channel is the new growth frontier.
BX.risk: A prolonged period where exits do not happen - no realisations means no performance fees and unhappy limited partners.
BX.implied: A high multiple of distributable earnings implies fundraising and realisations both normalise upward.
BX.debate: Bulls say permanent capital plus retail distribution is a structural growth story. Bears point at commercial real estate marks and a slow exit environment.
BX.disprove: Fundraising slowing; net accrued performance revenue declining; real estate fund redemptions rising; realisations staying frozen.

UBER.what: Runs marketplaces for ride-hailing, food delivery and freight, matching drivers and couriers with consumers.
UBER.rev: Mobility ~55% of revenue, delivery ~35%, freight the rest. Advertising is a small but very high-margin growth line. US and Canada ~45%.
UBER.gm: Take rate around 20-30% of gross bookings depending on segment. The marginal trip costs Uber almost nothing - the cost is driver incentives.
UBER.mgmt: Dara Khosrowshahi is CEO. Insider ownership small; the company reached genuine GAAP profitability in 2023-24.
UBER.comp: Lyft in US rides, DoorDash in delivery, Grab and Didi internationally, and Waymo in autonomy - as both partner and threat.
UBER.moat: Liquidity network effects in each city - more drivers means shorter waits means more riders - plus scale in routing and payments.
UBER.ind: Ride-hailing and delivery are both still growing double digits; autonomy is the structural wildcard.
UBER.risk: Autonomous fleets owned by Waymo or Tesla bypassing the Uber network entirely, turning it into a demand aggregator with no pricing power.
UBER.implied: The valuation implies bookings keep compounding at mid-to-high teens with margin expansion and a benign autonomy outcome.
UBER.debate: Bulls say Uber becomes the demand layer for every autonomous fleet. Bears say the fleets will go direct and Uber owns no vehicles.
UBER.disprove: Waymo or a rival launching a consumer app at scale in Ubers core cities; mobility bookings growth slowing; driver incentive costs rising; take rate falling.
